node.label: Alfred W. Crosby
node.date_label: The Columbian Exchange 1972 · Virgin Soil Epidemics 1976 · Ecological Imperialism 1986 · coverage through 2000
node.description: A historian of the biological consequences of European expansion. The Columbian Exchange (1972) followed pathogens, plants and animals between the Americas and the Old World after 1492, and 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) defined epidemics among peoples who, as Jones (2003, pp. 703–704) quotes the definition, 'have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them' (the 1976 article itself is unread). Ecological Imperialism (1986) starts from the fact that 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation', asks why 'the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion', and suggests that 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component': crops, livestock, weeds and diseases helped Europeans make temperate 'Neo-Europes'. Later critics charge the model with ecological determinism and argue that the virgin-soil idea was flattened into a claim that Indigenous Americans had 'no immunity'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred W. Crosby (1931–2018); The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972); 'Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America' (William and Mary Quarterly, 1976); Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986); 'The Past and Present of Environmental History' (American Historical Review, 1995). Readings: Miller's review (1987); Cook (1990); Cronon (1993); Subrahmanyam (1997); later, Jones (2003), McNeill (2003) and Isenberg (2013).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Ecological Imperialism as its prologue states the argument (pp. 1–7 read, with the contents and acknowledgments, in the publisher's sample of the 2004 second edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Columbian Exchange (1972), 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) and the 1995 AHR essay are unread: the 1972 book is characterised from Cook (1990) and McNeill (2003), and the 1976 wording is quoted as Jones (2003) quotes it. His 1978 American Heritage essay on New England, read in full, states the disease argument in his own words: 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless.' He is not presented as the founder of environmental history: the ASEH's own history lists him among several 'founding members' with Worster, Flader and Opie, and in 1982 among 'the already widely known historians'; he thanks William McNeill, who 'read the whole thing in first draft'. Contested readings: in period, Subrahmanyam (1997) calls the books 'oft-cited (and oft-criticized)', while Miller (1987) finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component'. Later, McNeill (2003) records that 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough'; Isenberg (2013) judges that his analysis 'devolved into little more than ecological determinism'; Jones (2003) argues that the virgin-soil model 'has been misunderstood and misrepresented', that the 1976 article itself stressed malnutrition and 'the social chaos generated by European colonization', and that Crosby's other writings stressed lack of immunity. These are later readings, not evidence for the edges. The 2004 preface, in which he calls Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario', is a later self-reading and is not used.

proposed_edges.relationship: Introduced organisms and pathogens as causes in colonial history: the Columbian exchange (1972) and ecological imperialism (1986)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Crosby's own statement, Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue (pp. 1–7 read; 2004-edition pagination). It opens: 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation' (p. 2), and names 'what I shall call the Neo-Europes' (p. 2). Underlying the pull of these lands 'were factors perhaps best described as biogeographical' (p. 5). 'European flora and fauna, including human beings, can thrive in these regions if the competition is not too fierce'; 'Perhaps European humans have triumphed because of their superiority in arms, organization, and fanaticism, but what in heaven's name is the reason that the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion? Perhaps the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). The contents give chapters 'Weeds' (145), 'Animals' (171) and 'Ills' (195). His 1978 American Heritage essay on Plymouth (web text read in full; no print pages) makes the disease argument for New England: 'Disease was among the commodities, and in this trade the Indians would come off second best'; 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless'; the Pilgrims survived 'thanks more to biology than religion'. In-period reception inside the field: Cronon's 1993 ASEH address (read) turns the two books into lessons of environmental history, 'When people migrate from one ecosystem to another, they carry with them other organisms—plants, animals, microbes—whose success or failure in the new location is often crucial in determining the success or failure of the migration' (p. 8) and 'Beware of bugs that come from afar' (p. 10), both footnoted to The Columbian Exchange and Ecological Imperialism (nn. 16, 25, p. 22). Cook's 1990 essay, read, takes The Columbian Exchange as the model for an ecological reading of Canadian contact: 'As Alfred W. Crosbie [sic], Jr., demonstrated so brilliantly nearly two decades ago ... contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13, n. 35). Miller's 1987 review (Medical History, read in full) calls the book 'a vividly written account of ecological transition' and finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component' (p. 374). The ASEH's history page (undated institutional account, read) records him commenting on the keynote at the society's first conference (Irvine, 1982) and lists him among 'founding members of our society such as Don Worster, Susan Flader, Alfred Crosby, and Opie himself'. A contribution, not a founding: no text read calls him the founder. Melville's adaptation of his question to Mexico (1994) is recorded in the existing melville_plague note, not rechecked. McNeill (2003, pp. 24, 33) and Isenberg (2013, p. 86), with their criticism of determinism, are later readings, not evidence for this edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: ecological_exchange ('Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange'; works: Ecological Imperialism, A Plague of Sheep) holds Crosby with Melville and its focus, 'Crosby's temperate settler environments', is exactly the checked prologue. colonial_property is Cronon's property strand; colonial_conservation is Grove and Carruthers.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ecological change at world scale: the biological expansion of Europe and the making of Neo-Europes, 900–1900 (1986)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The scale and question of Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue and contents (read; 2004-edition pagination). Other peoples expanded into adjacent lands, but 'Europeans, in contrast, seem to have leapfrogged around the globe' to Neo-Europes, 'lands thousands of kilometers from Europe and from each other' (p. 2); the book runs from 'The Norse and the Crusaders' and 'The Fortunate Isles' through 'Winds' to 'New Zealand' (contents, pp. xi–xii), and asks whether 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). He thanks 'William McNeill, who read the whole thing in first draft' (acknowledgments, p. xxii); McNeill is the world-history synthesiser on the global entry. In-period uptake by connected history: Subrahmanyam (1997, p. 738, re-read) lists among early modern shifts 'travel, discovery and colonization as leading to an ecological shift of global dimensions', and his note 10 points to 'the oft-cited (and oft-criticized) works of Alfred Crosby (The Columbian Exchange, and Ecological Imperialism)', adding that Grove's Green Imperialism 'pays far greater attention to Asia than does Crosby'. A contribution, not a founding, and a resource with stated limits: Subrahmanyam's own note marks it as criticised and as giving Asia less attention than Grove. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: McNeill (2003, p. 32) calls it 'Perhaps the best-known among the thematically defined global-scale environmental histories'; Crosby's 2004 preface names Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it' (pp. xvii, xx).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No global strand holds him. world is McNeill's Rise of the West synthesis; connected is Subrahmanyam's own strand, in which Crosby is only a cited resource; capitalism is Wolf's. global/world is the nearest fit (large-scale synthesis; McNeill read the draft) if the editor prefers a strand. A reviewer could instead add a strand at release, for example 'Biological expansion and ecological change at world scale' (Crosby, with Grove as the comparison Subrahmanyam draws).

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed: the evidence is not strong enough. The virgin-soil argument is about disease, but the 1976 article is unread, and the only in-period text read from medical history is Miller's 1987 review in Medical History, which reviews the book rather than showing uptake. The strong reception is Jones's 'Virgin Soils Revisited' (2003), a post-2000 critique from the history of medicine. The medicalhistory entry has no strand on epidemics and depopulation (colonial_medicine is Vaughan's power-and-medicine strand). A later extension could add a strand on disease and conquest with Jones as the critic.

Not proposed. The Indigenous history entry is built on Indigenous authority over research and Indigenous-authored histories; no in-period Indigenous reading of Crosby was read. Jones (2003, p. 705) warns that attributing depopulation 'to irresistible genetic and microbial forces' risks 'supporting racial theories of historical development', but that is a later reading and not an Indigenous historian's response. An edge here would assert a contribution the checked texts do not show.

Considered because Cook's 1990 essay (read, p. 13) uses The Columbian Exchange to recast Canadian contact as 'the interaction of different ecologies', and Wynn (2004, p. 41, in the canon evidence file) notes Crosby's claim that introduced diseases were 'the shock troops' of conquest. Not proposed: one in-period text, and it is an environmental-history manifesto, not a fur-trade or Native–newcomer study; the contact_wendat_representation strand (Trigger, Delâge, Dickason) was not checked for citations of Crosby. Open question for the editor (see NOTES).

Not proposed. The link is Crosby's 2004 preface (read), which calls The Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it'. It is post-2000 and a self-reading; Pomeranz's 2000 introduction (pp. 3–27, read for 1.130) was not checked for a citation of Crosby.

Not proposed. edge_112 reads 'Crosby and Melville connect introduced organisms with colonial expansion; Grove traces conservation through colonial networks'. Unlike edge_063 for Pomeranz (1.130), it names three scholars at different scales and is the field-to-field route; its evidence note already says their books 'provide resources' and that this 'does not prove that all global historians adopted them'. Edge 2 adds Crosby's own directed contribution and rests on the same Subrahmanyam note plus the prologue. Melville and Grove have no person entries, so removing Crosby's name would leave an unbalanced label. If the editor wants the 1.130 pattern, a neutral relabel is 'Introduced organisms, conquest and colonial networks: environmental history as a route beyond national containers', with source_ids unchanged.

new_sources.title: Alfred W. Crosby, “Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America,” William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser., 33, no. 2 (April 1976): 289–299.
new_sources.citation: Alfred W. Crosby, “Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America,” William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser., 33, no. 2 (1976): 289–299. doi:10.2307/1922166.

verification.note: Article unread: JSTOR returned a script challenge and OpenAlex (W1977541766) lists no open copy. Crossref 10.2307/1922166: William and Mary Quarterly 33(2), April 1976, first page 289; PubMed 11633588 (no abstract) gives 33:289–99. The words quoted in the atlas are Crosby's as quoted in Jones (2003), not checked against the original page: the definition, 'Virgin soil epidemics are those in which the populations at risk have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them and are therefore immunologically almost defenseless' (p. 289; Jones 703–704); the conclusion, 'The scientific community inclines towards the view that Native Americans have no special susceptibility to Old World diseases that cannot be attributed to environmental influences, and probably never did have' (p. 291; Jones 719). Jones also cites p. 292 for environmental factors (lack of childhood exposure, malnutrition, social chaos) and pp. 293–299 for specific factors. Fix pass 2026-10-13 (sol-review-1.131): the definition was re-checked in the JSTOR copy of Jones 2003 (text layer, pp. 703–704: 'As Crosby defined them in 1976, "Virgin soil epidemics are those in which the populations at risk have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them and are therefore immunologically almost defenseless"'); the node text names Jones as the witness at the point of quotation.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period article: identity checked; wording known only through a later critic's quotation.

new_sources.title: Alfred W. Crosby, “‘God … Would Destroy Them, and Give Their Country to Another People …’,” American Heritage 29, no. 6 (October/November 1978).
new_sources.citation: Alfred W. Crosby, “‘God … Would Destroy Them, and Give Their Country to Another People …’,” American Heritage 29, no. 6 (October/November 1978).

verification.note: Full essay read in the American Heritage online archive (byline Alfred W. Crosby; October/November 1978, volume 29, issue 6). The web text has no print page numbers; Jones (2003, n. 47) cites p. 39. Quoted: 'Disease was among the commodities, and in this trade the Indians would come off second best'; Europe 'had all the advantages of her disadvantages: an arsenal of diseases'; 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless'; the Pilgrims 'had survived and were getting stronger, thanks more to biology than religion'. Jones (2003, n. 47) cites this essay as one where Crosby 'emphasized the lack of immunity without discussing contributing social factors'. A popular-magazine essay, not a scholarly article.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1978) statement of the disease argument in Crosby's own words.

new_sources.title: Alfred W. Crosby, “The Past and Present of Environmental History,” American Historical Review 100, no. 4 (October 1995): 1177–1189.
new_sources.citation: Alfred W. Crosby, “The Past and Present of Environmental History,” American Historical Review 100, no. 4 (1995): 1177–1189. doi:10.1086/ahr/100.4.1177.

verification.note: Essay unread: Oxford Academic returned 403 and OpenAlex (W1970450249) lists no open copy. Crossref 10.1086/ahr/100.4.1177: AHR 100(4), October 1995, 1177–1189. ERIC abstract EJ519028 (read) says it 'Maintains that, although 18th-Century historians understand the significance of environmental influences, the concept of environmental history did not emerge until the mid-1900s' and 'Discusses the influence of Earth Day, Rachel Carson's "Silent Spring," and the landing of humans on the moon'. Two sentences are quoted by Sedrez in the AHR Conversation of 2008 (AHR 113:5, p. 1433, read): environmental historians had founded 'their own sect, the American Society for Environmental History, with its own journal', and 'the last ten years of the AHR includes more pages on film than on environmental history. Environmental history exists as an independent subdivision of the discipline, but it remains a minor one' (both p. 1188). Hoffmann, same page, says the essay 'still assumed that state records, scientific reports, policy debates, and other attributes of modernity were essential to research in it'. McNeill (2003, p. 18, n. 51) notes that Steinberg's 'and especially Crosby's essays briefly touch on works pertaining to regions beyond the U.S.'

new_sources.scope_note: In-period self-account of the field: identity, abstract and two quoted sentences only.

new_sources.title: Robert Miller, review of Alfred W. Crosby, Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986), Medical History 31, no. 3 (July 1987): 373–374.
new_sources.citation: Robert Miller, review of Crosby, Ecological Imperialism (1986), Medical History 31, no. 3 (1987): 373–374. doi:10.1017/S0025727300047062.

verification.note: Review read in full in the free Cambridge Core PDF (Crossref: Medical History 31(3), July 1987, 373–374; reviewer Robert Miller, Institute of Archaeology, London). Crosby documents the impact of 'what he calls the "portmanteau biota" of Old World crops, livestock, weeds, people, and pathogens' (p. 373); indigenous societies 'initially able to resist European military technology on nearly equal terms succumbed to hunger and disease', with malnutrition magnifying disease (p. 373); 'Crosby is in general conservative when it comes to estimating mortality from disease in post-contact history and is careful to take account of other social and biological factors that favoured the emergence of neo-Europes'; 'this is not just a study of disease, but a vividly written account of ecological transition, and Crosby is careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component' (p. 374). The reviewer also queries mortality rates drawn from 'partly theological narratives' (p. 374).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1987) review in a medical-history journal; a reading against the determinism charge.

new_sources.title: Ramsay Cook, “Cabbages Not Kings: Towards an Ecological Interpretation of Early Canadian History,” Journal of Canadian Studies 25, no. 4 (1990–91): 5–16.
new_sources.citation: Ramsay Cook, “Cabbages Not Kings: Towards an Ecological Interpretation of Early Canadian History,” Journal of Canadian Studies 25, no. 4 (1990–91): 5–16. doi:10.3138/jcs.25.4.5.

verification.note: Project MUSE PDF (University of Saskatchewan access, downloaded 2026-10-13 for the canon evidence file) re-read at p. 13 and note 35. Crossref 10.3138/jcs.25.4.5: JCS 25(4), issued January 1991, 5–16. 'Contact between Europe and North America, then, must be understood in the widest possible terms'; 'As Alfred W. Crosbie [sic], Jr., demonstrated so brilliantly nearly two decades ago, in his Columbian Exchange The Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492, contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments. Biological exchange in the form of pathogens that caused epidemic disease in populations where no immunity existed was perhaps the most spectacularly devastating consequence of contact. But the exchange of plants and animals was no less significant' (p. 13). Note 35 cites The Columbian Exchange (Greenwood, 1972) and Larocque (1982) on European diseases among Indigenous peoples in Quebec.

new_sources.title: David S. Jones, “Virgin Soils Revisited,” William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser., 60, no. 4 (October 2003): 703–742.
new_sources.citation: David S. Jones, “Virgin Soils Revisited,” William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser., 60, no. 4 (2003): 703–742. doi:10.2307/3491697.

verification.note: Later reading. JSTOR copy read as posted in an MITx course on edX (courses.edx.org asset 'VirginSoilWMQ'), pp. 703–711 and 718–720 closely, the rest searched for 'Crosby'. Crossref 10.2307/3491697: WMQ 60(4), October 2003, from p. 703. Jones quotes Crosby's 1976 definition (pp. 703–704). 'Even as Crosby's model of virgin soil epidemics remains a central theme of the historiography of the Americas, it has been misunderstood and misrepresented. Crosby actually downplayed the "genetic weakness hypothesis" and instead emphasized the many environmental factors that might have contributed to American Indian susceptibility to Old World diseases, including lack of childhood exposure, malnutrition, and the social chaos generated by European colonization' (p. 704). Historians 'have often reduced the complexity of Crosby's model to vague claims that American Indians had "no immunity"' (p. 704). Writers who 'attribute depopulation to irresistible genetic and microbial forces ... risk being interpreted as supporting racial theories of historical development' (p. 705). Crosby 'later described how thousands of years of disease exposure in Eurasia had created an Old World "superman"' (p. 707; the paragraph's n. 12 cites Ecological Imperialism, p. 34). 'McNeill, Crosby, and other historians utilized virgin soil theory' to restore causation (p. 711). Crosby's opening assertion of immunological defencelessness 'and the Darwinian tone of his other work jarred with the article's concluding emphasis on environmental causes of Indian susceptibility'; 'Crosby's work has been cited as both proof of immunological weakness and as evidence against it' (p. 719).

new_sources.scope_note: Later reading (2003), labelled as such: the main critique of the virgin-soil model.

new_sources.title: J. R. McNeill, “Observations on the Nature and Culture of Environmental History,” History and Theory 42, no. 4 (2003): 5–43.
new_sources.citation: J. R. McNeill, “Observations on the Nature and Culture of Environmental History,” History and Theory 42, no. 4 (2003): 5–43. doi:10.1046/j.1468-2303.2003.00255.x.

verification.note: Later reading. Copy hosted on williamcronon.net (downloaded 2026-10-13 for the canon evidence file); pp. 18–19, 24, 32–33 and 42 re-read for Crosby, page assignment from running heads. Crossref 10.1046/j.1468-2303.2003.00255.x. 'the American historians, especially Worster, Cronon, and Crosby, were read almost wherever environmental history aroused interest' (p. 19). The Columbian Exchange is 'one of the landmark works in environmental history' (p. 24). Ecological Imperialism is 'Perhaps the best-known among the thematically defined global-scale environmental histories' (p. 32) and 'contains one of the most elegant arguments found anywhere in environmental history'; 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough' (p. 33). Crosby 'did not have much to say about the transplanting of agronomic practice' (p. 42). Other drafts in this batch may cite McNeill 2003 under their own ids; merge at build if so.

new_sources.scope_note: Later reading (2003), labelled as such: standing and the agency critique.

new_sources.title: Andrew C. Isenberg, “From the Periphery to the Center: North American Environmental History,” Global Environment 6, no. 12 (2013): 80–101.
new_sources.citation: Andrew C. Isenberg, “From the Periphery to the Center: North American Environmental History,” Global Environment 6, no. 12 (2013): 80–101. doi:10.3197/ge.2013.061205.

verification.note: Later reading. Full text from environmentandsociety.org (downloaded 2026-10-13 for the canon evidence file); pp. 85–86 and n. 13 re-read. Crossref 10.3197/ge.2013.061205. 'The materialist approach was exemplified by the work of Alfred W. Crosby' (p. 85). 'As Crosby expanded the scope of his analysis, he increasingly depicted people as utterly at the mercy of ecological forces'; he quotes Ecological Imperialism (1986, p. 192, per n. 13) that European colonists 'were seldom masters of the biological changes they triggered' and that 'their role was less often a matter of judgment and choice than of being downstream of a bursting dam'; 'In short, over the course of two decades Crosby's analysis devolved into little more than ecological determinism' (p. 86). The 1986 passage is known here only through this quotation.

Quoted: 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation'; 'Europeans, in contrast, seem to have leapfrogged around the globe'; 'what I shall call the Neo-Europes, lands thousands of kilometers from Europe and from each other' (p. 2); 'factors perhaps best described as biogeographical' (p. 5); 'European flora and fauna, including human beings, can thrive in these regions if the competition is not too fierce'; 'what in heaven's name is the reason that the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion? Perhaps the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). Contents: 'The Norse and the Crusaders' (41), 'The Fortunate Isles' (70), 'Winds' (104), 'Weeds' (145), 'Animals' (171), 'Ills' (195), 'New Zealand' (217), 'Explanations' (269), 'Conclusion' (294). The 2004 preface (later) calls Pomeranz's The Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' (p. xvii, n.) and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it' (p. xx).
